# Kontext: EHL Finale (TUM.ai EHL Munich 2026, 10.–11.10.) – BMW Challenge

## Projekt
- Lokaler Ordner: ~/Documents/00_Events/EHL Finale
- Team-Repo: github.com/eklavyagoyal/ehl-finale-munich-submission (privat, Branch main, Teamkollegen pushen auch, vor Push immer fetchen/rebasen)
- Challenge: KI-App, die aus Kundenfeedback, BMW-Daten und Webrecherche Kundenanforderungen für das Nachfolgemodell (1er/5er/7er; EU/CN/US) ableitet, priorisiert und den Produktmanager entscheiden lässt (freigeben/ablehnen/bearbeiten). Ein Audit Trail protokolliert alles.
- Alle Infos zur Challenge stehen in docs/challenge/brief.md (Mission, Scope, Deliverables, 8 Pflichtfelder pro Requirement, BMW-Prozess mit Aufteilung KI vs. Mensch)

## Repo-Struktur (main)
- docs/README.md: Inhaltsverzeichnis
- docs/challenge/brief.md und sources/ (Briefing-PDF, 3 Slides)
- docs/datasets/: README (Übersicht, Abdeckung, Auffälligkeiten), customer-feedback.md, customer-studies.md, sales-volumes.md, option-lists/{F70-1-series,G60-5-series,G70-7-series}.md
- docs/bmw-pm-interview/: Notizen aus dem Gespräch mit dem BMW-Produktmanager (von Eklavya)
- data/: BMW-Rohdaten (8 Dateien aus Google Drive), per .gitignore NICHT im Repo
- .claude/settings.json und .entire/: lokal, gitignored (jeder richtet Entire selbst ein)

## Wichtige Erkenntnisse aus den Daten
- Feedback-Dateien: 1 Zeile pro Klassifizierung, nicht pro Feedback, also nach ID deduplizieren
- Kein Kundenfeedback für China und Deutschland; 5er/7er-Feedback kommt zu ~90 % aus den USA; Quellen B/C/D nur USA
- 1er (F70): nur Verkäufe in EU und Rest der Welt (keine in CN/US), nur Verbrenner
- G68 (5er Langversion, China) nur in der Kundenstudie und den Sales-Zahlen
- Kundenstudie: CN/EU = Mittelwerte (vermutlich Skala 1–10), USA = Verteilung auf 7-Punkte-Skala, nicht direkt vergleichbar, keine Stichprobengrößen
- Sales-Zahlen ohne Aufteilung nach Antrieb; 5er G60+G68 zusammengefasst
- OptionLists = deutsche Preislisten (Juli 2026); 7er-Ausstattungsdaten nur für 4 von 7 Modellen

## Entire (hack.entire.io/ehl-munich-2026)
- CLI 0.11.4 per Homebrew installiert; in EHL Finale aktiviert (Agent claude-code, Telemetrie an)
- `entire doctor` ist OK, aber: noch nicht eingeloggt (`entire login` selbst ausführen), 0 Checkpoints bisher
- Sessions nur im Repo- oder Worktree-Ordner starten; beim Commit „Commit mit Session verknüpfen?“ mit yes beantworten
- entire.io: Eklavya muss die GitHub App installieren und das Repo importieren

## Nächster Schritt
- Worktree mit eigenem Branch für die Entwicklung anlegen
- Dort fehlen data/, .claude/ und .entire/: data/ hineinkopieren (kein Symlink, den deckt /data/ in der .gitignore nicht ab), im Worktree `entire enable --agent claude-code` ausführen
- Dann Demo-Scope festlegen (Fahrzeug und Markt) und die Architektur planen

# Docs

Everything we received from BMW for the EHL Munich 2026 final (TUM.ai): the challenge, the data and the conversation with BMW, sorted.

**Start here:** [challenge/brief.md](challenge/brief.md) holds the full challenge (mission, scope, deliverables, BMW's process) in one file.

## Structure

```
docs/
├── README.md                          ← you are here
├── challenge/
│   ├── brief.md                       ← THE challenge: briefing + mission text + slides, consolidated
│   └── sources/                       ← originals from BMW
│       ├── BMW_Hackathon_Briefing_Short.pdf
│       ├── slide-data-and-sources.png
│       ├── slide-billions-of-findings-to-one-vehicle.webp
│       └── slide-the-process.webp

│   ├── customer-studies.md            ← F70_G60_G68_G70_customer_studies.xlsx (CN/EU means, US distributions)
│   ├── sales-volumes.md               ← sales_volumes.xlsx (full tables)
│   └── option-lists/                  ← *_OptionList.PDF extracted to Markdown (DE price lists, July 2026)
│       ├── F70-1-series.md

```

## Where to find what

| Question | Go to |

| Where does BMW expect AI vs human review? | [brief.md § 9 Process](challenge/brief.md#9-bmws-requirements-process-s5) |

# BMW Challenge — AI for Product Decision Making

Everything BMW gave us about the challenge, consolidated in one place (EHL Munich 2026 final, TUM.ai, 10–11 Oct 2026).

**Sources** (originals in [`sources/`](sources/)):

| # | Source | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| S1 | [`BMW_Hackathon_Briefing_Short.pdf`](sources/BMW_Hackathon_Briefing_Short.pdf) | Official 2-page briefing (BMW Group) |
| S2 | Detailed mission text (shared by BMW, pasted by the team) | Sections 1–5: mission, scope, "make it yours", deliverables |
| S3 | [`slide-data-and-sources.png`](sources/slide-data-and-sources.png) | Table "Data and sources — provided data (per vehicle)" |
| S4 | [`slide-billions-of-findings-to-one-vehicle.webp`](sources/slide-billions-of-findings-to-one-vehicle.webp) | Slide "From billions of findings to one BMW vehicle" |
| S5 | [`slide-the-process.webp`](sources/slide-the-process.webp) | Slide "The process" (BMW's requirements workflow) |

Where S1 and S2 differ in wording or emphasis, both are kept and marked.

---

## 1. The challenge in one paragraph

*What should the next generation of a BMW vehicle offer its customers?* Build an AI-powered application that helps product managers (PMs) **derive, justify and prioritize customer requirements for a successor vehicle**. Ground the proposals in customer feedback, BMW product and sales data, and relevant web research, while keeping **the PM firmly in control of every decision**. (S1)

## 2. Why this matters (S1)

- Defining a new vehicle generation means understanding what customers value today **and** anticipating what they will value when the successor reaches the market.
- PMs turn large volumes of customer feedback, market signals, competitor information and product data into well-founded product requirements.
- Today this work is largely **manual, time-consuming and hard to trace consistently**.
- AI could help PMs identify relevant insights, formulate requirements and justify prioritization decisions more efficiently, while keeping **evidence, assumptions and uncertainties transparent and under human control**.

## 3. Mission

### 3.1 Short version (S1)

Develop an application that helps PMs **define, explain and prioritize customer-facing requirements for the successor of an existing BMW vehicle line**.

- **Vehicles:** BMW 1 Series, 5 Series, 7 Series, or a combination.
- **Markets:** Europe, China, the United States, or any subset that best demonstrates the approach.
- **Time horizon:** think **3–5 years ahead**. Which customer needs and expectations should shape the next generation?
- Make clear **where conclusions rest on available evidence and where they rely on forward-looking assumptions**.
- For each vehicle BMW provides **customer feedback, equipment data, sales volumes and a customer study**. Teams may enrich these with external sources (competitor information, reviews, market or technology trends).
- BMW cares about **how the solution turns diverse information into actionable PM insights and makes its reasoning transparent**, not about a specific workflow or technical architecture.

### 3.2 Detailed version (S2, section 1 "Your mission")

Build an AI-powered application that ingests heterogeneous data, derives customer requirements for a vehicle, prioritizes them, and puts a PM in the loop at the decisions that matter. The app should be able to:

1. **Ingest** the provided data and enrich it with structured knowledge from the web.
2. **Extract signals** such as recurring complaints, unmet needs, competitor advantages and market trends, **each linked to its sources**.
3. **Derive requirements** from those findings: clear, actionable, customer-facing and realistic.
4. **Prioritize** them with a logic we define and can explain.
5. **Involve the PM** to approve, reject, edit or challenge requirements, along with the rationale and evidence behind them.
6. **Record everything in an audit trail**: a complete, chronological record of all actions, changes and access events within the system.

## 4. Scope (S2, section 2)

| In scope: customer requirements on the product | Out of scope |
| --- | --- |
| Features and equipment | Regulatory and homologation requirements (e.g. safety, emissions, type approval) |
| Comfort and space | Technical and engineering requirements (e.g. component specs, architecture, supplier topics) |
| Usability | Pricing, business case and cost calculation. **Cost or effort may be used as a rough prioritization factor.** |
| Infotainment and digital services | |
| Design and quality perception | |
| Driving experience | |
| Range and charging **as experienced by the customer** | |
| Variant and package offering, etc. | |

S1 says the same in short form: focus on **customer value** rather than engineering specifications, regulatory requirements or detailed business-case calculations.

## 5. Make it yours

- Demonstrate the application for **at least one derivative in one market**. Don't design it as a one-off: it should be **adaptable to other BMW vehicles and markets**. The remaining datasets and scenarios are available for optional testing. (S2)
- The challenge is broad on purpose. Focus where the team can contribute most, for example (S1 + S2):
  - going deep on **web research** and turning external information into usable evidence,
  - integrating and interpreting the **provided BMW data**,
  - uncovering customer insights, formulating compelling requirements, improving prioritization,
  - designing an effective **human-in-the-loop** experience.
- Not every capability needs the same maturity, but **show how the chosen focus connects to the full path from evidence to PM decision**. (S2)
- Consider how the concept scales across vehicle lines, markets and future product decisions. (S1)
- **What BMW values (S1):** trustworthy sources, transparent reasoning, thoughtful prioritization, and a clear understanding of **uncertainty and conflicting evidence**.

## 6. Deliverables

### 6.1 What to demonstrate (S1)

- **A concept and working prototype** showing how AI supports the identification, formulation and prioritization of customer-facing requirements, using the provided data and, where relevant, external sources.
- **A representative set of requirements supported by clear evidence and reasoning.** Show how customer feedback, product data, market signals or competitor insights translate into requirements, and explain the factors driving their prioritization.
- **A transparent decision-support experience** that lets PMs review, challenge, modify, approve or reject AI proposals, with evidence, assumptions, uncertainties and key decisions visible and traceable throughout.

### 6.2 Expected deliverables (S2, section 5)

> S2 jumps from section 3 to section 5; its section 4 is empty in the source.

1. **Concept and demonstrable prototype** of an AI-powered product-requirements application that processes heterogeneous inputs, derives product requirements, supports prioritization and integrates human review.
2. **Structured sample list of derived product requirements.** Every requirement needs all of these fields:
   - [ ] Unique identifier
   - [ ] Clear, actionable description
   - [ ] Linked findings and sources
   - [ ] Priority or score
   - [ ] Applied prioritization rationale
   - [ ] Evidence level
   - [ ] Key future-facing assumptions and uncertainties
   - [ ] Current decision status
3. **Clearly defined end-to-end workflow** showing how inputs become proposed and prioritized requirements, **which activities the AI performs autonomously, and where human review is mandatory**.
4. **Demonstrable audit trail** that makes each requirement traceable from its findings and sources through consolidation, scoring, prioritization and human decision-making. It must record changes to requirement **content, scores, priorities, evidence and status**, including **who or what** initiated each change, **when**, and the **documented rationale**.

> Teams choose their own technical approach, architecture, prioritization logic and UX. The deliverables describe capabilities and outcomes, not a prescribed design. They can be one integrated solution or a set of connected concepts, prototypes, models and visualizations. (S2)

## 7. Provided data (S3)

"Provided data (per vehicle)":

| Dataset | What it contains | What it is good for | Our file(s) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Customer verbatims** | Free-text customer feedback on the current vehicle | Pain points, unmet needs, what customers love and must not lose | `*_feedback_hackathon.xlsx` |
| **Equipment list** | Standard and optional equipment by trim and market | What the car offers today, gaps against competitors | `*_OptionList.PDF` |
| **Sales volumes** | Units by powertrain and region | Where the car sells, which powertrains matter, where it underperforms | `sales_volumes.xlsx` |
| **Customer study** | Customer ratings in various categories | How customers perceive, like/dislike and rate different components of a car | `F70_G60_G68_G70_customer_studies.xlsx` |

Schemas, value distributions and quirks of each file: [`../datasets/`](../datasets/README.md).

## 8. BMW's framing: from findings to one car (S4)

![From billions of findings to one BMW vehicle](sources/slide-billions-of-findings-to-one-vehicle.webp)

**1 billion findings › 1,000 requirements › one car.**

> **Customer requirement = customer-relevant attribute of a car.**

- **Example findings (raw customer voice):** "Charging takes too long." · "The NEW XPENG." · "Too many menus." · "Ugly kidney grille." · "I love the design." · "Too much plastic." · "More rear space, please." · "Uncomfortable seats." · "The app should just work." · "Very nice exterior colors." · "Tesla and GROK"
- **Example requirement themes (word cloud):** affordable, easy updates, data privacy, safety, joy of driving, flexible storage, everyday space, efficiency, connected, design, great sound, easy charging, reliable software, clear displays, easy entry, seat ventilation, home charging, art app, **intuitive UX**, iconic design, comfortable seats, smooth ride, fast charging, fast app response, sport wheels, real-world range, easy parking, heated seats, long battery life, personalized, carbon roof, simple maintenance, clear navigation, low running costs, dynamic, room for family, sustainable, easy child seat fit, electric, physical controls, **premium feel**, **range**
- Visual: "Future BMW sedan" (AI concept visual).

Takeaway: the job is **condensing many noisy, overlapping findings into a manageable set of customer-relevant attributes**. The findings mix complaints, praise, competitor mentions (XPENG, Tesla, Grok) and trends.

## 9. BMW's requirements process (S5)

![The process](sources/slide-the-process.webp)

Five stages, left to right. The slide marks each box with a **robot icon (AI)** and/or a **person icon (human)**:

| Stage | Box | Content on the slide | AI | Human |
| --- | --- | --- | :---: | :---: |
| **1. Situation analysis** | Baseline | Previous BMW model · BMW portfolio · Sales volume | ✓ | ✓ |
| | Competition | | ✓ | |
| | Customer / public feedback | | ✓ | |
| | Product and global trends | | ✓ | |
| **2. Structure & context** | Classify, cluster, contextualize | "AI standardizes findings, identifies duplicates, groups themes and connects insights" | ✓ | |
| | All potential requirements (0/1) | e.g. BEV powertrain, cooler, seat ventilation, … → **"Implement requirement?"** (binary yes/no) | | |
| **3. Requirements definition** | Specification and quantification | "Define measurable targets and acceptance criteria" | ✓ | ✓ |
| | Metric specification | e.g. *Range: 600 or 700 mi?* · *Cooler: for how many bottles?* · *Seat ventilation: fast enough?* | | |
| | (unlabeled column, likely domains) | Exterior · Interior · Powertrain · Driver assistance · … | | |
| **4. Prioritization** | | Customer · Business · … | ✓ | ✓ |
| **5. Documentation** | Requirements tracking | (cycle icon: continuous tracking) | ✓ | |

Reading of the slide (our interpretation):

- **AI-only (autonomous) steps:** gathering competition, feedback and trends; classifying, clustering and de-duplicating findings; documentation and requirements tracking.
- **AI + human (review mandatory) steps:** setting the baseline, specifying and quantifying requirements, prioritization. These map directly onto deliverable 6.2 #3 ("where human review is mandatory").
- Requirements go through two levels: first a **binary decision** (implement: 0/1), then a **metric specification** (how much / how good).
- Prioritization weighs **customer** value against **business** factors.

## 10. Related inputs from BMW people

- Notes from the conversation with a BMW product manager: [`../bmw-pm-interview/`](../bmw-pm-interview/). It covers the signal channels, the prioritization questions BMW actually asks, the 1–2 year iteration loop, and how lines between vehicle classes are drawn.

## 11. Quick facts

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Vehicles (e-codes) | **F70** = 1 Series · **G60** = 5 Series sedan · **G68** = 5 Series long wheelbase (China; customer study only) · **G70** = 7 Series |
| Markets in focus | Europe, China, USA (any subset) |
| Horizon | Successor vehicle, 3–5 years ahead |
| Minimum demo | ≥ 1 derivative in ≥ 1 market, built to generalize |
| Hard constraints | Customer-facing requirements only; no regulatory, engineering or pricing work |
| Must-haves | Requirement list (8 fields), E2E workflow with AI-vs-human split, audit trail, PM-in-the-loop prototype |
# Datasets

Documentation of the data BMW provided for the challenge: schemas, value distributions, coverage and quirks.

> **The raw files are not in git.** They live locally in `/data/` (ignored via `.gitignore`). Download them from the BMW challenge Google Drive folder:
> <https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/REDACTED>
> These docs describe the files and show only short examples, no raw dumps (except the small sales and CN/EU study tables).

## Inventory

| Dataset (BMW name) | File in `data/` | Size | Vehicles | Doc |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| Customer verbatims | `F70_feedback_hackathon.xlsx` | 472 KB | 1 Series F70 | [customer-feedback.md](customer-feedback.md) |
| | `G60_feedback_hackathon.xlsx` | 706 KB | 5 Series G60 | 〃 |
| | `G70_feedback_hackathon.xlsx` | 615 KB | 7 Series G70 | 〃 |

# BMW Product Manager Discussion — Groundwork

Source: [Original conversation notes](conversation-with-bmw-prod-manager.md).

This document organizes the discussion into a foundation for our next steps. The source is a set of rough notes; examples and estimates below should be read in that context.

## Core idea

Product requirements develop through an ongoing process of gathering signals, understanding their relevance, checking feasibility, and refining a vehicle-specific draft. Decisions depend on the market, customer group, vehicle class, engineering possibilities, and business constraints.

The manager emphasized that this process keeps looping. The timeline mentioned was roughly **one to two years**, with repeated reviews and deeper investigation of internal feedback.

## Where the signals come from

The discussion identified several inputs:

- **Social media:** customer feedback and requests.
- **Agencies:** another channel for input; their specific role was not detailed.
- **Competitors:** comparisons of what other vehicles offer and how quickly competitors may catch up.
- **Market contacts:** people who understand local culture, customer habits, and everyday usability.
- **Internal feedback and usage data:** deeper feedback reviews, plus data supplied through the app and use of the car.

Before prioritizing a request, the manager pointed to the number of people behind it, its sources, source reliability, the relevant region, and the functionality involved. A verification loop was also mentioned, although its exact steps were not described.

## How the work progresses

The notes suggest the following flow, with repeated loops between stages:

1. **Collect signals** from the different channels.
2. **Assess relevance and priority**, including the market and any quality issues.
3. **Speak with engineering early** to establish rough feasibility: can the requirement actually be implemented?
4. **Align the inputs and constraints** into a first draft for the specific car.
5. **Revisit the draft**, investigate internal feedback more deeply, and update requirements as new information arrives.

The initial engineering conversation is an early feasibility check. The notes do not describe a formal approval process or fixed gates between these stages.

## What shapes a decision

| Area | Questions raised in the discussion |
| --- | --- |
| Evidence | How many people are asking? Which sources support the request, and how reliable are they? |
| Market fit | Which region is relevant? Does the requirement fit local culture and how people use the car? |
| Functionality and quality | What functionality is involved? What quality issues need attention? |
| Vehicle fit | Is the request reasonable for this class of car? Does it belong in a higher class? How do vehicle size and budget affect the decision? |
| Engineering and R&D | Can it be implemented? Is it feasible from an R&D perspective? |
| Cost and business case | Is it feasible cost-wise? What are the budget, volume, and margin considerations? |
| Reuse | Can the requirement or feature be used in other vehicles? |
| Timing and flexibility | How quickly could the requirement change? How does that fit the development timeline, and can the team stay flexible? |
| Competition | How does the vehicle compare with competitors? How quickly could they catch up? |

Finding the data needed to answer these questions was itself raised as a challenge.

## Differences between markets and vehicle lines

The manager described drawing boundaries between vehicle lines as tricky. No fixed rule was given; feasibility, vehicle size, budget, customer group, and competitor comparisons all influence the decision.

The notes include illustrative customer examples: younger people in relation to the **1 Series**, and entrepreneurs in relation to the **5 or 7 Series**. These are discussion examples, not a complete segmentation model.

The discussion also referred to **“product genesis”** and the contribution of people in each market who understand its culture and basic usability needs. Their input helps assess whether a requirement fits that market.

## Timeline and when the loop ends

When asked about the timeline and criteria for ending the loop, the answer remained somewhat unspecified. The discussion raised R&D feasibility, reuse across vehicles, budget, changing requirements, functionality, competition, region, volume, and margins as relevant considerations.

The notes do not establish a fixed number of iterations, a precise stopping rule, or a final decision owner.

## Internal data collection

When asked how data is collected internally, the manager referred to the **app** and **use of the car**, through which users supply data. The notes end before this process is explained further.

The specific data collected, how it is accessed, and how it feeds into prioritization remain unclear.

## Open questions for the next stage

- What does the verification loop check, and what evidence is sufficient to prioritize a request?
- How are conflicting signals from different sources and markets resolved?
- How are requests allocated between vehicle lines in practice?
- What determines when a draft is ready and the iteration loop can end? Who makes that decision?
- Which data is available for assessing demand, feasibility, cost, volume, and margins?
- How are app and vehicle-usage data connected to customer feedback and product decisions?

These are follow-up questions derived from gaps in the notes. They are not additional requirements stated by the manager.

> **One row = one classification, not one feedback.** A verbatim that mentions several topics appears once per topic, with the same `ID` and the same text. Always count unique `ID`s when you count feedbacks. All rows of one ID carry identical text (verified).

## Gotchas for the pipeline

- De-duplicate by `ID` before any text analysis (embeddings, LLM extraction) and keep the classification rows as labels.
- `Source` affects how to read the text: B is second-hand paraphrase ("Customer stated…"), while C and D wrap the answer in survey boilerplate that should be stripped.
- Source C encodes **severity** in the text ("very minor problem" … "very serious problem"), which could feed into scoring.
- Countries are very unbalanced. Any market-level claim needs the counts shown next to it, and statements about China cannot be backed by feedback.
- The VFC taxonomy (226 topics × 84 natures across all files) is BMW's own classification. It can serve as a starting cluster structure or as ground truth for checking our own clustering.

Layout (observed): long format, 934 rows, columns `A` = label, `B` = `"% of column, sample base"`, `C` = **BMW 5 Series G60**, `D` = **BMW 7 Series G70** (the header label carries a trailing space: `'BMW 7 Series G70 '`). Vehicle headers appear only once, in row 1. Each attribute block has 9 rows:

```
<Attribute name>
Sample total      1       1
I Hate It         0.005   0.005
A Failure         0.007   0.011
Unsatisfactory    …
Satisfactory      …
Excellent         …
Delightful        …
I Love It         …        (each block sums to 1.0, verified)
```

**Scale (7-point):** I Hate It < A Failure < Unsatisfactory < Satisfactory < Excellent < Delightful < I Love It. Useful aggregates are the top-2 box (Delightful + I Love It), the bottom-3 box (I Hate It + A Failure + Unsatisfactory), or a weighted mean (1–7).

### The 103 attributes (in sheet order, grouped by us)

- **Exterior:** Overall exterior styling · Size/ proportions · Appearance of tires/ wheels · Exterior door handles · Headlight/ taillight design · Sound of doors/ trunk/ hatch shutting
- **Driving:** Overall driving performance · Ground clearance · Riding comfort · Turning radius · Handling/Maneuverability · If applicable: 4WD/AWD performance · Off-Road capability · Overall power and pickup · Acceleration from stop · Passing capability
- **Interior design & quality:** Overall interior styling/ aesthetics · Interior colors · Interior trim and finish · Interior lighting · Overall interior workmanship · Quality of seat materials · Quality of interior materials · Interior door handles
- **Seats, space & practicality:** Overall comfort of the seats · Comfort of front seat · Comfort of 2nd row seat · Overall interior design / layout · Ease of front seat entry · Front seat roominess · Ease of 2nd row seat entry · 2nd row seat roominess · Passenger seating capacity · Interior roominess · Interior storage · Trunk lid/ tailgate and liftgate operations · Ease of loading/unloading cargo · Cargo capacity/usefulness · Instrument panel (IP) · Cupholders · Provides a sense of wellbeing · Overall interior versatility/seat stowaway · Driver seat adjustability · Passenger seat adjustability
- **Climate & audio:** Overall performance of climate control system · Heater performance · Air conditioner performance · Operation of heater/ AC controls · Overall performance of sound system · Design and integration of speakers · Audio clarity · Bass performance
- **Controls, NVH & quality:** Placement/ ease of reading and using controls · Intuitiveness of controls · Overall noise/vibration/harshness · Overall vehicle sound · Active noise cancellation · Freedom from squeaks and rattles · Sound of engine · Freedom from wind and road noise · Smoothness of transmission · Overall impression of durability/reliability · Solid vehicle construction · Freedom from electrical problems
- **Safety & visibility:** Overall safety of the vehicle · Front visibility · Rear visibility · Braking · Warranty coverage · Headlight function/ brightness
- **Value & brand:** Technical innovations · Level of standard equipment · Overall value for money · Price/deal offered · Future trade-in or resale value · Gas or electric mileage (fuel economy) · Economical to own (cost of ownership) · Affordable to buy · Overall brand image · Reputation/prestige of manufacturer · Overall vehicle image
- **Driver assistance:** Overall driver assist features · If applicable: Backup system (camera, sensors, etc.) · Safety monitoring features (blind spot warning, lane departure warning, etc.) · Adaptive driving assists (lane keeping, cruise, braking)
- **HMI, infotainment & connectivity:** Overall driver-vehicle interaction (HMI) · If applicable: Navigation system · Bluetooth/ smartphone pairing · WiFi hotspot in vehicle · Mirroring of smartphone content on vehicle display · Place for phone · Phone charging · Ease of reading and using screen interface · Head-up Display · Position/ integration of displays in dashboard · Menu structure of infotainment system · If applicable: Interactive information system (e.g., OnStar, mbrace, iDrive) · Performance of voice recognition · Vehicle's Mobile App
- **Other:** Overall environmental friendliness · If applicable: Flat tire preparedness (spare, run flat, etc.) · If applicable: Sunroof/ moonroof · If applicable: Ease of customization

(The source spells "blid spot warning"; corrected above.)

## Gotchas for the pipeline

- The two sheets **cannot be compared directly**: CN/EU uses means on an inferred 10-point scale, the US uses distributions on a 7-point scale. Normalize within a sheet (rank, z-score, gap to the best vehicle) before combining.
- Attribute names differ between the sheets (e.g. "Quietness when driving" vs "Freedom from wind and road noise"), so a mapping table is needed to link them, and to link both to the feedback VFC topics.
- With no sample sizes, report study results as relative signals, not statistically tested ones.

# Plan: Wettbewerbsanalyse pro Fahrzeug und Markt

Kurz vorab zum Stand: Der Worktree liegt unter `.claude/worktrees/luis` auf dem Branch `luis-competitors`. `data/` ist hineinkopiert und eine lokale `.venv` mit pandas angelegt, beides gitignored. Den Branch habe ich `competitors` geschrieben statt `compeditors`. Er hat noch keinen Upstream, damit nichts versehentlich auf `main` landet. Beim ersten Push also `git push -u origin luis-competitors`, vorher fetchen und rebasen.

**Entire musst du im Worktree selbst aktivieren.** Der Session-Schutz hat mich den Befehl nicht ausführen lassen:

```bash
cd "/Users/luisdehlwes/Documents/00_Events/EHL Finale/.claude/worktrees/luis"
```
```bash
entire enable --agent claude-code
```

```bash
entire status
```

---

## Ziel

Für jede sinnvolle Kombi aus Fahrzeug und Markt soll klar sein, gegen welche Fahrzeuge der Nachfolger antritt und was deren Kunden und die Fachpresse loben oder kritisieren. Die Ergebnisse sollen so strukturiert sein, dass wir sie später direkt mit dem BMW-Feedback vergleichen können. Im BMW-Prozess ist das der Schritt „Competition“, den die KI eigenständig erledigen soll.

## 1. Scope: 7 Kombis statt 9

Der 1er wird in China und den USA nicht verkauft, deshalb fallen diese beiden Kombis weg. Den 5er gibt es in China nur als Langversion G68. Er bekommt deshalb eigene Wettbewerber: Langversionen und chinesische E-Limousinen.

Die Wettbewerber in der Tabelle sind **Hypothesen**. Die Webrecherche soll sie bestätigen oder korrigieren.

| Kombi | Vermutete Wettbewerber |
| --- | --- |
| **F70 · EU** | Mercedes A-Klasse, Audi A3 Sportback, VW Golf (GTI/R vs. M135), Mini; elektrische Kompakte als Ausblick |
| **G60 · EU** | Mercedes E-Klasse / EQE, Audi A6 / A6 e-tron, Tesla |
| **G60 · US** | E-Class, A6, Genesis G80, Lexus ES, Tesla Model S/3, Cadillac CT5 |
| **G68 · CN** | E-Klasse L, Audi A6L, Xiaomi SU7, NIO ET7, Zeekr, Huawei-Marken (Luxeed), BYD Han |
| **G70 · EU** | S-Klasse / EQS, Audi A8, Porsche Panamera |
| **G70 · US** | S-Class / EQS, Lexus LS, Genesis G90, Lucid Air, Tesla Model S |
| **G70 · CN** | S-Klasse / Maybach, Audi A8L, Maextro S800, NIO ET9, Hongqi |

**Blick 3–5 Jahre voraus:** Der Nachfolger tritt gegen die *nächste* Generation der Wettbewerber an. Angekündigte Modelle nehmen wir deshalb mit auf und markieren sie als zukunftsbezogene Annahme. Das zahlt direkt auf das Pflichtfeld „Annahmen und Unsicherheiten“ ein.

## 2. Drei Evidenz-Ebenen pro Kombi

| Ebene | Inhalt | Quelle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **(a) Ausstattung** | Nur kundenrelevante Punkte aus dem Scope: Displays und Bedienung, Fahrassistenz, Reichweite und Laden aus Kundensicht, Platz im Fond, Sitzkomfort, Serie vs. Option. **Kein Preisvergleich**, Preise sind out of scope. | Herstellerseiten, Tests |
| **(b) Kunden- und Pressefeedback** | Was an den Wettbewerbern gelobt und kritisiert wird. Das ist der Kern deiner Frage. | Fachpresse (Autocar, What Car, ADAC, Car and Driver, Edmunds …), Besitzerbewertungen, JD Power und Consumer Reports, wo verfügbar |
| **(c) BMW-Verbatims, die Wettbewerber nennen** | Mit wem die Kunden selbst vergleichen, plus direkte Vergleiche wie *„Mercedes hat die bessere Klimaanlage“* | Unsere Feedback-Dateien |

Zu Ebene (c) habe ich schon vorab gezählt: Die Zahlen sind **rohe Treffer einer Mustersuche** mit Fehltreffern, etwa „Golf“ im Sinne von Golftasche, „Competition“ als M-Ausstattung oder „other cars“.

| Datei | Rohtreffer | Was auffällt |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| F70 | ~92 | VW, Mercedes, Audi, Mini; fast alles aus GB |
| G60 | ~178 | Tesla 62 (alle USA, vor allem Laden und Reichweite), Mercedes 32, Audi 25 |
| G70 | ~197 | Mercedes 98 (USA), Tesla 34, Porsche und Lexus je 13 |

Ein LLM klassifiziert diese Treffer sauber. Für die USA ist die Ebene stark, für die EU dünn, und **für China gibt es sie gar nicht**.

## 3. Kern des Designs: Vergleichbarkeit

Damit wir später vergleichen können, bekommt jeder Wettbewerber-Befund dieselbe Struktur wie das BMW-Feedback:

- **Feedback-Typ:** Likes, Wants, Difficult to Use, Defect, plus „Wettbewerber-Vorteil“, „BMW-Vorteil“ oder „Gleichstand“.
- **Thema:** ca. 15 grobe Themen, zum Beispiel Infotainment und Bedienung, Fahrassistenz, Laden und Reichweite, Fahrkomfort, Sitze, Platz, Innenraumqualität, Klima und Akustik. Die 226 BMW-Topics sind für Pressetexte zu fein. Wir mappen sie auf diese groben Themen, die Studien-Attribute ebenso.
- **Pro Befund:** Fahrzeug, Markt, Wettbewerbsmodell, Aussage (paraphrasiert), Quellen-URL, Quellentyp, Datum, Evidenz-Stufe.
- **Evidenz-Stufen:** A = viele Kundenaussagen, B = Fachpresse-Test, C = Herstellerangabe, D = Ankündigung oder Prognose.

Diese Felder speisen später direkt die Pflichtfelder „Linked findings and sources“ und „Evidence level“.

## 4. Ablauf und Zeitbudget

1. **Taxonomie und Schema** festlegen: Themenliste, Mappings, JSON-Schema (ca. 30 Min.).
2. **Verbatims klassifizieren:** Ein Agent geht die rund 470 Rohtreffer durch, verwirft Fehltreffer und ordnet Wettbewerber, Typ und Thema zu.
3. **Leichter Recherche-Durchgang für alle 7 Kombis:** ein Recherche-Agent pro Kombi, parallel, alle mit demselben Ausgabeschema (ca. 1–1,5 Std.).
4. **Zusammenführen:** eine Vergleichsmatrix aus Thema × Wettbewerber × Markt, die zeigt, wo BMW vorne liegt und wo hinten.
5. **Tiefer Durchgang** nur für die Demo-Kombi des Teams.

Die Ergebnisse kommen ins Repo, nicht nach `data/`, das ist gitignored:

- `docs/competitors/`: Markdown-Zusammenfassung pro Kombi
- `competitors/findings.json`: der Datensatz für die App
- `competitors/themes.json`: die Mappings

## 5. Risiken

- **China:** Die besten Quellen wären chinesische Besitzerplattformen wie Autohome oder Dongchedi. Die sind schwer abrufbar und auf Chinesisch. Ausweichen würden wir auf englische China-Fachmedien (CarNewsChina, CnEVPost) und JD Power China. Diese Daten sind dünner, das schreiben wir offen dazu.
- **Skalen:** Externe Bewertungen nutzen andere Skalen als die BMW-Studie. Wir verwenden sie nur als relatives Signal und vermischen keine Zahlen.
- **Urheberrecht:** Wir speichern nur Paraphrasen, URLs und kurze Zitate. Review-Seiten werden nicht massenhaft gescrapt.

---

## Was du entscheiden musst

1. **Tiefe:** Leichter Durchgang für alle 7 Kombis, nur ein tiefer Durchgang für die Demo-Kombi, oder beides? Ich empfehle beides.
2. **Breite:** Nur deutsche Premium-Wettbewerber, oder auch Tesla, Lexus, Genesis, Lucid und chinesische EV-Marken? Für China sind die chinesischen Marken Pflicht.
3. **Format:** Datensatz für die App plus kurze Markdown-Zusammenfassung, oder nur Markdown?
4. **Demo-Kombi:** Zu welcher Kombi tendiert das Team? Davon hängt ab, wo der tiefe Durchgang hingeht.

# Wettbewerbsanalyse: mein Vorschlag

Ich würde den Plan in zwei Durchgängen umsetzen.

**1. Breiter Durchgang für alle 7 Kombis.** Er braucht die Demo-Entscheidung noch nicht.

- **Wettbewerber breit fassen:** deutsche Premium-Marken, dazu Tesla, Lexus, Genesis und Lucid, und für China die chinesischen E-Marken. Ohne die fehlt in China und den USA die halbe Konkurrenz.
- **Pro Kombi:** wer die Wettbewerber sind, heute und in der nächsten Generation, was Kunden und Presse an ihnen loben und kritisieren, und wo sie in den Scope-Themen besser oder schlechter als BMW sind.
- **Dazu die BMW-Verbatims, die Wettbewerber nennen,** sauber per LLM klassifiziert.
- **Ausgabe:** `competitors/findings.json` als Datensatz für die App, `competitors/themes.json` als Mapping und eine kurze Zusammenfassung pro Kombi unter `docs/competitors/`.

**2. Tiefer Durchgang für das Fahrzeug, das ihr in der Demo zeigt.** Ich würde den **5er** nehmen: Er ist das Volumenmodell und das einzige, das in **allen drei Märkten** relevant ist (G60 in EU/US, G68 in China). Das passt zu „EU, China, USA bleibt“.

Für die Story ist das stark: In China gibt es kein Kundenfeedback, die Wettbewerbsrecherche füllt genau diese Lücke. Das zeigt sichtbar, wie Webrecherche zu Evidenz wird.

**Konkret würde ich jetzt so loslegen:**

1. Themenliste und Schema festlegen (ca. 30 Min.)
2. Parallel 7 Recherche-Agenten starten, je einen pro Kombi, dazu einen, der die Verbatims klassifiziert
3. Alles zusammenführen, committen und auf `luis-competitors` pushen

7 kombis oder 7er kombi?

„7 Kombis“ heißt sieben Kombinationen aus Fahrzeug und Markt, nicht der 7er. Es sind diese:

| Fahrzeug | EU | China | USA |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **1er (F70)** | 1 | — | — |
| **5er (G60 / G68)** | 2 | 3 (G68, Langversion) | 4 |
| **7er (G70)** | 5 | 6 | 7 |

Theoretisch wären es 3 × 3 = 9. Der 1er wird aber in China und den USA nicht verkauft, deshalb bleiben 7.

# VFC level3 values that describe perceived value / equipment gaps regardless of the level2 component.

    "Dislike: price-performance ratio": "equipment_value",
    "Like: price-performance ratio": "equipment_value",
    "Vehicle equipment: not available": "equipment_value",
    "Vehicle equipment: not standard / too costly": "equipment_value",
    "Like: vehicle equipment": "equipment_value",
}

FEEDBACK_TYPES = ["Likes", "Wants", "Difficult to Use", "Defect"]
COMPARISON = ["competitor_advantage", "bmw_advantage", "parity"]
EVIDENCE_TIERS = {
    "A": "Customer voice: owner review, owner forum post, owner survey",
    "B": "Professional test/review by automotive press",
    "C": "Manufacturer specification or configurator",
    "D": "Announcement, leak or forecast (forward-looking assumption)",
}


def main(feedback_path: str) -> None:
    df = pd.read_excel(feedback_path, dtype=str)
    counts = df.groupby("Vfc level2 Name")["ID"].nunique()

    mapping = {topic: theme for theme, topics in VFC_TO_THEME.items() for topic in topics}
    dupes = [t for theme, topics in VFC_TO_THEME.items() for t in topics if list(mapping).count(t) > 1]
    assert not dupes, dupes

    unmapped = sorted(t for t in counts.index if t not in mapping)
    unknown = sorted(t for t in mapping if t not in counts.index)
    if unmapped:
        sys.exit(f"Unmapped VFC level2 topics: {unmapped}")
    if unknown:
        print(f"Note: mapped but absent from this file: {unknown}")

    theme_ids = {t[0] for t in THEMES}
    assert set(mapping.values()) <= theme_ids and set(LEVEL3_TO_THEME.values()) <= theme_ids

    out = {
        "version": 1,
        "description": "Shared theme taxonomy so BMW G60 feedback and competitor findings can be compared. "
        "BMW feedback: theme = LEVEL3 override if present, else VFC level2 mapping; empty level2 -> unclassified.",
        "themes": [{"id": i, "label_de": de, "scope": desc} for i, de, desc in THEMES],
        "feedback_types": FEEDBACK_TYPES,
        "comparison_values": COMPARISON,
        "evidence_tiers": EVIDENCE_TIERS,
        "vfc_level3_to_theme": LEVEL3_TO_THEME,
        "vfc_level2_to_theme": {t: mapping[t] for t in sorted(mapping)},
        "vfc_level2_g60_feedback_counts": {t: int(n) for t, n in counts.sort_values(ascending=False).items()},
    }
    target = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "themes.json"
    target.write_text(json.dumps(out, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2) + "\n")

    per_theme = pd.Series({t: 0 for t in theme_ids})
    for topic, n in counts.items():
        per_theme[mapping[topic]] += n
    print(per_theme.sort_values(ascending=False).to_string())
    print(f"wrote {target}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(sys.argv[1])

input.content:
# Competitor research — BMW 5 Series (G60, China: G68)

Competitor vehicles for the 5 Series and what their customers and the press say about them, structured so it can be compared with BMW's own G60 feedback.

| Market | BMW baseline | Competitor feedback sources |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EU | G60 feedback (thin, mostly GB/SE/DK) + DE option list | owner reviews, owner forums, press tests |
| US | G60 feedback (rich, Sources A–D) | owner reviews, owner forums, press tests |
| CN | **G68** (long wheelbase) — no BMW feedback, so G68 owner reviews are collected from the web as baseline | Autohome / Dongchedi / Sohu / Yiche owner reviews, press |

## How comparability works

1. **Same theme axis.** [`themes.json`](themes.json) defines 18 coarse themes. Every BMW VFC level2 topic is mapped to one theme ([`tools/build_themes.py`](tools/build_themes.py)), and every competitor finding is tagged with a theme from the same list.
2. **Same feedback types** as BMW: `Likes`, `Wants`, `Difficult to Use`, `Defect`.
3. **One topic per record.** Like the BMW files (one row per classification), a review that covers three topics becomes three records sharing one `review_ref`. Count unique `review_ref`s, not records.
4. **Compare shares, not counts.** Competitor owner-review volume is far smaller than BMW's. Compare the sentiment mix per theme. The closest BMW baseline for competitor owner reviews is **BMW Source A** (owner reviews); Sources B–D (dealer/survey channels) have no competitor equivalent.
5. **Same generation.** All model years of the current generation count; the generation code is on every record.

## Files

| File | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `themes.json` | Theme taxonomy, VFC → theme mapping, feedback types, evidence tiers |
| `raw/<agent>.jsonl` | Records from one research agent (one JSON object per line) |
| `raw/<agent>.log.md` | What that agent searched, fetched, found and could not access |
| `tools/` | Scripts (theme build, merge, validation) |

## Record schema (`raw/*.jsonl`)

### `kind: "feedback"`: one statement about one theme

| Field | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `record_id` | str | `<agent>-F0001` |
| `review_ref` | str | `<agent>-R001`: groups records from the same review/post |
| `kind` | `"feedback"` | |
| `market` | `EU` \| `US` \| `CN` | |
| `country` | ISO-2 | country of the source/reviewer if known (`GB`, `DE`, `US`, `CN`, …) |
| `brand`, `model`, `generation` | str | e.g. `Mercedes-Benz`, `E-Class`, `W214` |
| `model_year` | str \| null | |
| `powertrain` | `ICE` \| `PHEV` \| `BEV` \| `unknown` | |
| `source_type` | `owner_review` \| `owner_forum` \| `owner_survey` \| `press_review` | |
| `source_name` | str | e.g. `cars.com`, `Autohome`, `Car and Driver` |
| `url` | str | **a page the agent fetched itself** |
| `published` | `YYYY-MM` \| `YYYY` \| null | |
| `feedback_type` | `Likes` \| `Wants` \| `Difficult to Use` \| `Defect` | `Wants` = request/missing feature; `Difficult to Use` = usability pain or weak performance; `Defect` = something broken |
| `theme` | theme id | from `themes.json` |
| `vfc_level2` | str \| null | best-matching BMW VFC level2 topic (keys of `vfc_level2_to_theme`), if one fits well |
| `comparison` | `competitor_advantage` \| `bmw_advantage` \| `parity` \| null | only when the source explicitly compares with BMW / the 5 Series |
| `statement` | str | English paraphrase, 1–2 sentences, one topic, e.g. "Owner states the air suspension makes the ride very smooth on highways." |
| `quote` | str \| null | optional original-language excerpt, **under 15 words** |
| `language` | `en` \| `de` \| `zh` \| … | language of the source |
| `rating` | str \| null | e.g. `4/5` if the review carries one |
| `evidence_tier` | `A` \| `B` | A = customer voice, B = press |

### `kind: "equipment"`: one customer-facing feature of one vehicle in one market

`record_id` (`<agent>-E0001`), `kind`, `market`, `brand`, `model`, `generation`, `trim_scope` (e.g. `entry trim`, `all trims`, `i5 eDrive40`), `feature`, `theme`, `availability` (`standard` \| `optional` \| `not_available` \| `unknown`), `value` (e.g. `"270 kW DC peak"`), `source_type` (`manufacturer` \| `press_review`), `url`, `as_of` (`YYYY-MM`), `evidence_tier` (`C` \| `B`), `notes`.

### `kind: "competitor"`: why a vehicle is in the competitor set

`record_id` (`<agent>-C001`), `kind`, `market`, `brand`, `model`, `generation`, `powertrains`, `launched`, `rationale`, `next_generation` (announced successor/facelift, or null), `next_generation_evidence_tier` (`D`), `url`.

## Rules for collection

- Every record cites a URL that was actually fetched. Search snippets are not records. Zero results is a valid outcome; it gets logged.
- No CAPTCHA, login or bot-block workarounds. Known blocked: Edmunds (403), Reddit, What Car (paywall).
- Store paraphrases, not copied review text; quotes stay under 15 words.
- BMW verbatim text from `data/` never goes into committed files, only IDs and labels.

You are a research agent in a hackathon team (TUM.ai EHL Munich 2026, BMW challenge). Goal: collect competitor data and competitor customer feedback for the BMW 5 Series (G60) so it can be compared with BMW's own customer feedback, theme by theme.

Working directory (git worktree): /Users/luisdehlwes/Documents/00_Events/EHL Finale/worktrees/luis-competitors
READ FIRST: competitors/README.md (record schema, fixed equipment feature ids, rules) and competitors/themes.json (theme ids; the keys of `vfc_level2_to_theme` are the allowed `vfc_level2` values).

Theme ids (use exactly these): powertrain_performance, range_charging_efficiency, ride_handling, adas_parking, hmi_infotainment, connectivity_app_digital, access_locking, seats_comfort, climate, space_practicality, interior_design_quality, exterior_design, lighting_visibility, audio_acoustics, safety, equipment_value, overall_quality_ownership, unclassified.
feedback_type: exactly one of Likes | Wants | Difficult to Use | Defect.

HARD RULES
1. Every record must cite a URL you fetched yourself with WebFetch in this task, and the fetched content must support the record. WebSearch snippets are NOT evidence. Never invent, generalize or "typical-case" a review. If a source yields nothing, log it and move on. Fewer real records beat many weak ones; record counts are limits, not targets.
2. WebFetch returns a model-written summary of the page. In your WebFetch prompt, ask it to list EACH individual review/post separately with model year, powertrain/trim, date, rating, and what the person liked / disliked / wanted, and to state how many reviews are visible. Only build records from output that is anchored to individual reviews (or, for press, to the specific article).
3. One topic per record; records from the same review/post/article share a `review_ref`.
4. Paraphrase in English ("Owner states ...", "Reviewer states ..."). Optional `quote` under 15 words. Never copy review text.
5. No CAPTCHA / login / paywall / bot-block workarounds. Known blocked: edmunds.com (403), reddit.com, whatcar.com (402). On 403/402/captcha: log and move on.
6. Budget: at most ~45 WebFetch calls and ~15 WebSearch calls in total.
7. Only the CURRENT generation of each model counts (any model year of that generation). Put the generation code on every record.
8. Write outputs with the Write tool. Rewrite your JSONL file after finishing each model so partial results survive. One JSON object per line, UTF-8.
9. Do not modify any other files. Do not run git. Helper scripts (if any) go to /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-luisdehlwes-Documents-00-Events-EHL-Finale/17a2c20e-7947-4abe-8706-20475727794d/scratchpad/

YOUR ASSIGNMENT — agent key `us_mercedes`, market US
Models:
- Mercedes-Benz E-Class sedan, generation W214 (MY2024+; E350, E450, AMG E53 Hybrid)
- Mercedes-Benz EQE sedan, generation V295 (MY2023+)
Produce:
(a) one `competitor` record per model (rationale: why it competes with the 5 Series / i5 in the US; note: BMW's own G60 US feedback mentions Mercedes ~30 times).
(b) `feedback` records: owner reviews and owner forum posts (up to ~40 per model, as many as are real), plus 2–3 press reviews per model split into theme records (evidence_tier B). Look specifically for direct comparison tests vs BMW 5 Series / i5 and fill `comparison`.
(c) `equipment` records for the US-market versions, using the fixed feature ids F01–F20 from the README (skip BEV features for ICE and vice versa; `unknown` is fine).
Source ideas: cars.com consumer reviews (e.g. https://www.cars.com/research/mercedes_benz-e_class-2025/consumer-reviews/ — also try 2024/2026 and the EQE pages), kbb.com consumer reviews (e.g. https://www.kbb.com/mercedes-benz/e-class/2024/consumer-reviews/), mbworld.org forums (W214 / EQE sections), caranddriver.com, motortrend.com, consumerreports.org (free parts), jdpower.com, mbusa.com (specs).

OUTPUTS
- competitors/raw/us_mercedes.jsonl
- competitors/raw/us_mercedes.log.md: models covered; per source: URL tried, status (ok / 403 / empty / paywall), records produced; 3–5 headline findings per model (with themes); caveats.
Final reply (short): record counts per model and kind, sources that worked/failed, top 3 findings, anything suspicious.

"""Aggregate BMW G60 feedback onto the shared theme axis (counts only, no verbatim text).

Writes competitors/bmw_g60_theme_profile.csv with one row per
market x source x engine type x theme x feedback type, counting unique feedback IDs.

Usage: .venv/bin/python competitors/tools/bmw_baseline.py data/G60_feedback_hackathon.xlsx
"""

import json
import sys
import warnings
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
EUROPE = {"GB", "SE", "DK", "FI", "NO", "FR", "ES", "LV", "DE", "IT", "NL", "BE", "AT", "CH", "PL"}


def market(country: str) -> str:
    if country == "US":
        return "US"
    if country in EUROPE:
        return "EU"
    return "other"


def main(feedback_path: str) -> None:
    themes = json.loads((ROOT / "themes.json").read_text())
    l2_map = themes["vfc_level2_to_theme"]
    l3_map = themes["vfc_level3_to_theme"]

    df = pd.read_excel(feedback_path, dtype=str)
    df["Vfc level2 Name"] = df["Vfc level2 Name"].str.replace("\xa0", " ")

    def theme(row) -> str:
        if row["Vfc level3 Name"] in l3_map:
            return l3_map[row["Vfc level3 Name"]]
        return l2_map.get(row["Vfc level2 Name"], "unclassified")

    df["theme"] = df.apply(theme, axis=1)
    df["market"] = df["Country"].map(market)
    df["engine"] = df["Engine Type"].replace({"BEVE": "BEV"})
    df["feedback_type"] = df["Feedback Type"].fillna("none")

    profile = (
        df.drop_duplicates(["ID", "theme", "feedback_type"])
        .groupby(["market", "Source", "engine", "theme", "feedback_type"])["ID"]
        .nunique()
        .rename("feedbacks")
        .reset_index()
        .rename(columns={"Source": "source"})
    )
    out = ROOT / "bmw_g60_theme_profile.csv"
    profile.to_csv(out, index=False)

    pivot = profile.pivot_table(index="theme", columns="market", values="feedbacks", aggfunc="sum", fill_value=0)
    print(pivot.sort_values("US", ascending=False).to_string())
    print(f"wrote {out} ({len(profile)} rows)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(sys.argv[1])

input.content:
"""Pull NHTSA owner complaints for the BMW 5 Series (G60) and its US competitors, map them to themes.

NHTSA complaints are the one customer channel measured the same way for every vehicle in the US,
so they give a like-for-like comparison of *what goes wrong* (almost all are defects).

Writes:
  nhtsa_us_complaints.csv      one row per complaint x theme (no complaint text, ODI number for lookup)
  nhtsa_us_theme_profile.csv   complaints per vehicle x theme, with share of the vehicle's complaints

Usage: .venv/bin/python competitors/tools/nhtsa.py
"""

import csv
import json
import re
import time
import urllib.parse
import urllib.request
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
API = "https://api.nhtsa.gov"

# vehicle key -> (label, make, model years, include regex on NHTSA model name, exclude regex)
VEHICLES = {
    "bmw_5_g60": ("BMW 5 Series (G60)", "BMW", range(2024, 2028), r"^(5\d0I|I5|5 SERIES)", r"GRAN TURISMO|^M5"),
    "mb_e_w214": ("Mercedes-Benz E-Class (W214)", "MERCEDES-BENZ", range(2024, 2028), r"^E[- ]?(CLASS|\d{3})", r"COUPE|CABRIOLET"),
    "mb_eqe_v295": ("Mercedes-Benz EQE sedan (V295)", "MERCEDES-BENZ", range(2023, 2028), r"^EQE", r"SUV"),
    "audi_a6_etron": ("Audi A6 e-tron (PPE)", "AUDI", range(2025, 2028), r"^(A6|S6).*E-TRON", r"$^"),
    "audi_a6_c9": ("Audi A6 (C9)", "AUDI", range(2026, 2028), r"^(A6|S6)\b", r"E-TRON|ALLROAD|AVANT|RS"),
    "tesla_model_3": ("Tesla Model 3 (Highland)", "TESLA", range(2024, 2028), r"^MODEL 3", r"$^"),
    "tesla_model_s": ("Tesla Model S (2021 refresh)", "TESLA", range(2021, 2028), r"^MODEL S", r"$^"),
    "genesis_g80": ("Genesis G80 (RG3)", "GENESIS", range(2021, 2028), r"G80", r"$^"),
    "lexus_es_7": ("Lexus ES (XZ10)", "LEXUS", range(2019, 2026), r"^ES", r"$^"),
    "cadillac_ct5": ("Cadillac CT5", "CADILLAC", range(2020, 2028), r"^CT5", r"$^"),
}

COMPONENT_THEME = [
    ("AIR BAG", "safety"), ("SEAT BELT", "safety"), ("CHILD SEAT", "safety"), ("SEATS", "seats_comfort"),
    ("STEERING", "ride_handling"), ("SERVICE BRAKES", "ride_handling"), ("PARKING BRAKE", "ride_handling"),
    ("SUSPENSION", "ride_handling"), ("TIRES", "ride_handling"), ("WHEELS", "ride_handling"),
    ("ENGINE", "powertrain_performance"), ("POWER TRAIN", "powertrain_performance"),
    ("FUEL/PROPULSION", "powertrain_performance"), ("HYBRID PROPULSION", "powertrain_performance"),
    ("FORWARD COLLISION", "adas_parking"), ("LANE DEPARTURE", "adas_parking"), ("BACK OVER", "adas_parking"),
    ("VISIBILITY", "lighting_visibility"), ("EXTERIOR LIGHTING", "lighting_visibility"),
    ("LATCHES/LOCKS", "access_locking"), ("STRUCTURE", "overall_quality_ownership"),
    ("EQUIPMENT", "overall_quality_ownership"),
]
# For ELECTRICAL SYSTEM / UNKNOWN OR OTHER / VEHICLE SPEED CONTROL the text decides (first match wins).
TEXT_THEME = [
    ("range_charging_efficiency", r"charg|high[- ]voltage|\bhv\b|traction battery|battery pack|range"),
    ("adas_parking", r"cruise|lane|collision|emergency brak|phantom|automatic brak|parking assist|park assist|camera|radar|sensor"),
    ("hmi_infotainment", r"screen|display|infotainment|idrive|mbux|touch ?screen|monitor|instrument cluster|navigation|head[- ]up"),
    ("connectivity_app_digital", r"carplay|android auto|bluetooth|\bapp\b|software update|over the air|\bota\b|wi-?fi|phone"),
    ("access_locking", r"door|lock|key|trunk|liftgate|tailgate|handle"),
    ("climate", r"a/c|air condition|heater|hvac|climate|defrost"),
    ("powertrain_performance", r"loss of (motive )?power|power loss|lost power|accelerat|propulsion|transmission|stall|shift"),
    ("overall_quality_ownership", r"12 ?v|12-volt|battery|electrical"),
]
TEXT_DECIDED = ("ELECTRICAL SYSTEM", "UNKNOWN OR OTHER", "VEHICLE SPEED CONTROL")


def get(path: str, **params) -> dict:
    url = f"{API}{path}?{urllib.parse.urlencode(params)}"
    for attempt in range(3):
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=30) as r:
                return json.load(r)
        except Exception as e:  # NHTSA returns 400 for unknown model/year combinations
            if attempt == 2:
                print(f"  ! {url}: {e}")
                return {"results": []}
            time.sleep(1.5)
    return {"results": []}


def themes_for(components: str, summary: str) -> list[str]:
    text = summary.lower()
    out = []
    for comp in [c.strip() for c in components.split(",") if c.strip()]:
        if comp.startswith(TEXT_DECIDED):
            theme = next((t for t, rx in TEXT_THEME if re.search(rx, text)), "overall_quality_ownership")
        else:
            theme = next((t for key, t in COMPONENT_THEME if comp.startswith(key)), "overall_quality_ownership")
        if theme not in out:
            out.append(theme)
    return out or ["unclassified"]


def main() -> None:
    model_cache = {}
    rows = []
    for key, (label, make, years, inc, exc) in VEHICLES.items():
        seen = set()
        for year in years:
            if (make, year) not in model_cache:
                res = get("/products/vehicle/models", modelYear=year, make=make, issueType="c")["results"]
                model_cache[(make, year)] = sorted({r["model"] for r in res})
            models = [m for m in model_cache[(make, year)] if re.search(inc, m) and not re.search(exc, m)]
            for model in models:
                for c in get("/complaints/complaintsByVehicle", make=make, model=model, modelYear=year)["results"]:
                    odi = c["odiNumber"]
                    if odi in seen:
                        continue
                    summary = c.get("summary") or ""
                    if key == "mb_eqe_v295" and re.search(r"\bsuv\b", summary.lower()):
                        continue  # NHTSA mixes EQE sedan and EQE SUV in some buckets
                    seen.add(odi)
                    for theme in themes_for(c.get("components") or "", summary):
                        rows.append({
                            "vehicle_key": key, "vehicle": label, "make": make, "nhtsa_model": model, "model_year": year,
                            "odi_number": odi, "date_filed": c.get("dateComplaintFiled"), "components": c.get("components"),
                            "theme": theme, "crash": c.get("crash"), "fire": c.get("fire"),
                            "injuries": c.get("numberOfInjuries"),
                        })
                time.sleep(0.2)
            print(f"{label} MY{year}: models {models}")
        print(f"  -> {len(seen)} complaints")

    with (ROOT / "nhtsa_us_complaints.csv").open("w", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=list(rows[0]))
        w.writeheader()
        w.writerows(rows)

    complaints = defaultdict(set)
    per_theme = defaultdict(Counter)
    for r in rows:
        complaints[r["vehicle"]].add(r["odi_number"])
        per_theme[r["vehicle"]][r["theme"]] += 1
    with (ROOT / "nhtsa_us_theme_profile.csv").open("w", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["vehicle", "complaints_total", "theme", "complaints", "share_of_vehicle_complaints"])
        for veh, counter in per_theme.items():
            total = len(complaints[veh])
            for theme, n in counter.most_common():
                w.writerow([veh, total, theme, n, round(n / total, 3)])
    print({v: len(s) for v, s in complaints.items()})


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Per market x theme scorecard: BMW 5 Series vs its competitors.

Inputs: findings.jsonl (merge.py), bmw_g60_theme_profile.csv (bmw_baseline.py), nhtsa_us_theme_profile.csv (nhtsa.py)
Output: scorecard.csv with, per market and theme,
  - owner voice: share of negative statements (Difficult to Use + Defect) for BMW vs pooled competitors
      BMW baseline = G60 Source A owner reviews (EU/US) or G68 web owner reviews (CN)
  - head-to-head verdicts: explicit comparisons (web records + BMW verbatims naming a rival)
  - NHTSA (US only): share of complaints on the theme, BMW vs competitor median

Usage: .venv/bin/python competitors/tools/compare.py
"""

import csv
import json
import statistics
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
NEG = {"Difficult to Use", "Defect"}
TYPES = {"Likes", "Wants", "Difficult to Use", "Defect"}


def main() -> None:
    themes = [t["id"] for t in json.loads((ROOT / "themes.json").read_text())["themes"]]
    recs = [json.loads(line) for line in (ROOT / "findings.jsonl").read_text().splitlines() if line.strip()]

    owner = defaultdict(Counter)  # (market, side, theme) -> {neg, total}
    reviews = defaultdict(set)
    verdict = defaultdict(Counter)  # (market, theme) -> comparison counts
    for r in recs:
        if r["kind"] == "feedback":
            is_bmw = r["brand"] == "BMW"
            if r["source_type"] in ("owner_review", "owner_forum") and "nhtsa" not in r["source_name"].lower():
                side = "bmw" if is_bmw else "competitors"
                owner[(r["market"], side, r["theme"])]["total"] += 1
                owner[(r["market"], side, r["theme"])]["neg"] += r["feedback_type"] in NEG
                reviews[(r["market"], side, r["theme"])].add(r["review_ref"])
            if r.get("comparison") and not is_bmw:
                verdict[(r["market"], r["theme"])][r["comparison"]] += 1
        elif r["kind"] == "bmw_mention" and r["relation"] in ("competitor_advantage", "bmw_advantage", "parity"):
            mkt = "US" if r.get("country") == "US" else ("EU" if r.get("country") in {"GB", "SE", "DK", "FI", "NO", "FR", "ES", "LV"} else None)
            if mkt:
                verdict[(mkt, r["theme"])][r["relation"]] += 1

    # BMW G60 Source A owner reviews (EU/US) from the BMW data
    with (ROOT / "bmw_g60_theme_profile.csv").open() as f:
        for row in csv.DictReader(f):
            if row["source"] == "Source A" and row["market"] in ("EU", "US") and row["feedback_type"] in TYPES:
                key = (row["market"], "bmw", row["theme"])
                owner[key]["total"] += int(row["feedbacks"])
                owner[key]["neg"] += int(row["feedbacks"]) if row["feedback_type"] in NEG else 0

    nhtsa = defaultdict(dict)
    path = ROOT / "nhtsa_us_theme_profile.csv"
    if path.exists():
        with path.open() as f:
            for row in csv.DictReader(f):
                nhtsa[row["theme"]][row["vehicle"]] = float(row["share_of_vehicle_complaints"])
    nhtsa_vehicles = {v for d in nhtsa.values() for v in d}

    out = []
    for market in ("EU", "US", "CN"):
        for theme in themes:
            b, c = owner[(market, "bmw", theme)], owner[(market, "competitors", theme)]
            v = verdict[(market, theme)]
            row = {
                "market": market, "theme": theme,
                "bmw_owner_statements": b["total"],
                "bmw_owner_share_negative": round(b["neg"] / b["total"], 2) if b["total"] else "",
                "competitor_owner_statements": c["total"],
                "competitor_owner_reviews": len(reviews[(market, "competitors", theme)]),
                "competitor_owner_share_negative": round(c["neg"] / c["total"], 2) if c["total"] else "",
                "verdict_competitor_better": v["competitor_advantage"],
                "verdict_bmw_better": v["bmw_advantage"],
                "verdict_parity": v["parity"],
            }
            if market == "US" and nhtsa_vehicles:
                bmw_key = next((k for k in nhtsa_vehicles if k.startswith("BMW")), None)
                rivals = [nhtsa[theme].get(k, 0.0) for k in nhtsa_vehicles if k != bmw_key]
                row["nhtsa_bmw_share"] = nhtsa[theme].get(bmw_key, 0.0) if bmw_key else ""
                row["nhtsa_competitor_median_share"] = round(statistics.median(rivals), 3) if rivals else ""
            out.append(row)

    fields = list(out[0]) + ["nhtsa_bmw_share", "nhtsa_competitor_median_share"]
    fields = list(dict.fromkeys(fields))
    with (ROOT / "scorecard.csv").open("w", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fields)
        w.writeheader()
        w.writerows(out)
    print(f"wrote {ROOT / 'scorecard.csv'} ({len(out)} rows)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

1. **Besitzerstimmen:** der Anteil negativer Aussagen bei BMW gegenüber den Wettbewerbern, zusätzlich bereinigt um den Unterschied zwischen den Bewertungsplattformen.

import json

from pathlib import Path

        rec = json.loads(line)
        quote = rec.get("quote") or ""
        if quote and (len(quote.split()) >= 15 or len(quote) > 60):

            changed += 1
        lines.append(json.dumps(rec, ensure_ascii=False))

    print(f"{path.name}: {changed} quotes removed")

5	Cells written as **`a / b`** mean `a` unique BMW feedback IDs / `b` records. Count IDs, not records (one verbatim can carry several competitors or aspects).
6	
7	## Method
8	
9	1. Deduplicated 5,005 classification rows to **4,000 unique feedback IDs** (all rows of one ID have the same text).
10	2. Ran a broad regex prefilter in three passes:
11	   - Brand and model names, plus common misspellings.
12	   - Model codes (e.g. E 350, C-200) and KR/JP market names (Grandeur, Sonata, K8 …).
13	   - Generic comparison phrases ("compared to", "previous car", "other brands", "rivals", "switched from", "cross-shop" …).
14	   - Fixes made during the review: an `audi` pattern without a word boundary matched "audio", so it was corrected; `g wagon` and hyphenated model codes were added.
15	3. Every candidate text was read by hand (448 unique IDs across the passes). Discard categories:
16	   - regex false positives: VW Golf pattern on golf equipment, Samsung phones, substrings such as `etron`, non-Tesla charging networks, loaner/rental cars;
17	   - comparisons with BMW's own models or earlier BMW generations;
18	   - the BMW M/Competition trims;
19	   - generic overall superlatives against unnamed other cars;
20	   - generic automated-driving wishes that name no brand;
21	   - non-automotive brands such as phone makers.
22	4. Coding rules:
23	   - One record per (feedback ID, competitor, aspect).
24	   - Directional records (`competitor_advantage` / `bmw_advantage` / `parity`) are written per compared aspect.
25	   - `cross_shopped` is added when the customer says they considered or test drove the competitor. Its aspect is "Purchase consideration" when the compared aspect already has a directional record.
26	   - `previous_car` is used **only** when the customer says they came from the brand and makes no directional comparison.
27	   - Prior or concurrent ownership is tracked separately (table below), so it does not inflate `previous_car`.
28	   - Source B: only competitors raised by the customer count. Mentions made only by the call-centre writer were dropped.
29	5. Generic statements (`competitor_brand: "generic"`) are kept only when they make a specific comparison on an aspect.
30	   - The comparison target is "rivals", "other brands/makes", other cars in the segment, or other cars the customer has driven, and the statement names an aspect such as sound system, build quality or a driver-assist warning.
31	   - Brand groups that the customer names are kept as such: `Japanese brands`, `Korean brands`, `German brands`.
32	   - Statements that the customer is considering other brands, with no brand named, are kept as `generic` + `mention_only` + aspect "Considering other brands". Filter them out if you do not need them.
33	6. `theme` is the compared aspect, judged by hand. The BMW VFC level2 → theme mapping was used only as a hint.
34	7. `feedback_type` describes the BMW side of that aspect (Likes / Wants / Difficult to Use / Defect).
35	8. `engine_type` uses BEV for BMW's `BEVE`, consistent with `tools/bmw_baseline.py`.

# Competitor analysis: BMW 5 Series (G60, China G68)

Which vehicles the 5 Series successor competes with in **EU, US and China**, and what their customers and the press say about them. All findings use the **same theme axis as BMW's own feedback**, so BMW and competitors can be compared theme by theme.

Collected on 2026-10-10 by 8 web-research agents plus 1 classification run over BMW's G60 verbatims. Data, schema and scripts are in [`/competitors`](../../competitors/README.md).

## At a glance

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Records | **3,020** valid (0 rejected): 2,219 feedback statements, 494 equipment facts, 255 BMW-verbatim competitor mentions, 21 outlook items, 31 competitor-set entries |
| Competitor vehicles | 21 (current generations), plus BMW G68 owner reviews as China baseline |
| Extra channel | **NHTSA complaints** for the 5 Series and 9 US rivals (1,286 complaints), pulled the same way for every car |
| Source check | 8 of 8 randomly drawn records verified against their source page (Sohu ×3, cars.com ×2, KBB, GoingElectric, NHTSA) |

## Competitor set

| Market | Competitors covered | Main evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **EU** | Mercedes E-Class (W214), EQE (V295), Audi A6 (C9), A6 e-tron (PPE), Volvo ES90, Tesla Model S / Model 3, NIO ET7 | ADAC Autotests, AUTO BILD / AUTO ZEITUNG comparison tests vs 5er/i5, Auto Express (incl. Driver Power), carwow; owner voice thin (GoingElectric, autocentrum.pl) |
| **US** | Mercedes E-Class, EQE, Audi A6 (C9), A6 Sportback e-tron, Tesla Model S / Model 3, Genesis G80 (RG3), Lexus ES (XZ10 + 8th gen), Cadillac CT5 | cars.com and KBB owner reviews (≈ 450 statements), NHTSA complaints, KBB / cars.com / The Drive / Autoblog comparisons |
| **CN** | BMW 5 Series Li **G68** (baseline), Mercedes E-Class L (V214), Audi A6L (C8 L, new C9 L), Xiaomi SU7, NIO ET7, Zeekr 007, Luxeed S7, Stelato S9 | Sohu Auto owner reviews (≈ 750 statements, same platform for BMW and rivals), Autohome 530Li vs E 300 L instrumented test, CarNewsChina, CnEVPost |

Why these: German premium rivals are the classic cross-shops. Tesla is the brand BMW G60 customers name most (66 of 191 verbatims that mention a rival). Genesis, Lexus and Cadillac are the US value alternatives. Volvo ES90 and NIO ET7 are what European press tests against the i5. In China, Chinese NEV sedans in the same price band are positioned against the 5 Series Li.

## How to read the comparison

Comparisons are only made **within the same channel**:

| Channel | BMW side | Competitor side | Comparable? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Owner voice | G60 **Source A** owner reviews (EU/US) · G68 Sohu owner reviews (CN) | owner reviews / forums from the web | Directional. In CN it is like-for-like (same platform). In EU/US the platforms differ, so the scorecard also gives each theme's critical share **relative to that side's average** |
| Head-to-head verdicts | BMW verbatims that compare with a rival | press tests and owners that compare with the 5 Series / i5 | Yes. Counts who is judged better on a theme |
| Complaints (US) | NHTSA complaints, 5 Series MY2024+ | NHTSA complaints, 9 rivals | Yes, same source and method. Compare shares; volumes depend on fleet size |
| Press | BMW option list (DE), BMW US/CN specs | tests and spec pages | Equipment facts, 20 fixed features |

"Critical" = Wants + Difficult to Use + Defect (everything that is not a Like). Treat all shares as signals: most themes have 5–60 statements per side.

## Findings by market

### US

| Theme | Signal | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Charging & range** | Competitors ahead | Verdicts 23 : 10 for rivals. BMW owner critical share 0.80 vs 0.22 for rivals. 14 BMW verbatims single out Tesla Supercharger access. A6 e-tron: 800 V, 270 kW, 10–80 % in 21 min and up to 392 mi vs i5 205 kW / ~30 min |
| **Driver assistance** | Competitors ahead | Verdicts 19 : 3 for rivals (automated parking, sign recognition, collision warning). Cadillac CT5 has Super Cruise standard; on the G60 the Highway Assistant is optional |
| **Ride & handling** | BMW ahead | Verdicts 27 : 8 for BMW. Lowest relative critical share for BMW (−0.32). Press: BMW wins agility and steering vs G80, E-Class, EQE |
| **Overall quality** | BMW ahead in comparisons, but NHTSA flags brakes | Verdicts 22 : 7 for BMW (build quality, mostly vs Tesla). But 59 % of 5 Series NHTSA complaints concern brakes/stability (rival median 25 %), 22 of 49 tied to the integrated brake module recall |
| **Infotainment / controls** | Mixed | Verdicts 15 : 7 for rivals on features, yet press favours BMW's rotary controller over touch-only rivals. Lexus ES XZ10 owners hate its touchpad; the new ES brings back physical climate controls |
| **Connectivity & app** | Competitors ahead | BMW relative critical share +0.28 (CarPlay drops, app, remote functions); verdicts 7 : 1 for rivals |
| **Equipment value** | BMW ahead | Verdicts 9 : 3 for BMW. But rivals often include features as standard that BMW sells as options (ventilated seats standard on G80, CT5, A6) |

### EU

Owner voice is thin on both sides (BMW EU Source A: ~150 statements; competitors ~100), so **press verdicts carry the market**:

- **i5 wins both EV comparison tests**: vs EQE 350 (AUTO BILD, 635 : 612) and vs A6 e-tron Avant (AUTO ZEITUNG, 3,305 : 3,292). It wins on handling, boot, rear seat posture and price.
- **Rivals win on ride comfort and quietness**: E-Class estate (air suspension) beat the 520d Touring 3,322 : 3,294. EQE measured quieter (61 vs 63 dB), and the A6 e-tron's air suspension rides better than the i5 Touring.
- **Charging gap**: ES90 (800 V, ~300 kW, 10–80 % in 22 min) and A6 e-tron (270 kW, 23 min) vs i5 at 205 kW / 30 min. EU verdicts on charging 5 : 3 for rivals; BMW EU owners' most critical theme is charging (0.62).
- **Touch-only controls are the shared weakness of every rival**: no physical climate controls on E-Class, A6, A6 e-tron, ES90 or Teslas. AUTO ZEITUNG prefers iDrive's controller to Mercedes touch controls. Audi is bringing back steering-wheel rollers for MY2026.
- **Audi interior quality has slipped** (ADAC, AUTO ZEITUNG: hard plastics, piano black, rattles).

### China

The cleanest owner-voice comparison: G68 and its rivals are all reviewed on Sohu Auto.

- **Equipment value is the G68's weak spot, and rivals win every head-to-head**: verdicts 7 : 0 for rivals. G68 owners complain about cut equipment by trim: no ventilated seats on 525Li/530Li entry trims, sunroof that cannot open, stripped audio, paid remote start / remote climate, 3 months of free data. Audi A6L owners call their car better value. Chinese NEVs ship driver assistance and ventilated seats as standard where the i5 charges extra.
- **Design**: verdicts 6 : 0 for rivals. E-Class L owners rate its styling above the new 5 Series, and some did not consider the BMW because of its looks.
- **Driver assistance**: Huawei ADS (Luxeed S7, Stelato S9) and Zeekr highway assist are the most praised feature among NEV owners (rival relative critical share −0.22). Lidar is standard on SU7, 007 and S7, and the A6L e-tron uses Huawei NOA. The G68 offers L2 only, and China approved its first L3 cars in December 2025.
- **Charging**: 800–900 V is the norm in the class (Zeekr 007 10–80 % in ~10 min, Luxeed S7 30–80 % in ~12 min) vs i5 L 30–80 % in ~36 min.
- **Where the German trio is all weak**: high rear centre tunnel (G68, E-Class L, A6L). G68: brake squeal/judder (4 of 15 reviewers on one trim page), body roll (no rear anti-roll bar, confirmed by the Autohome test). A6L C8: jerky at low speed (11 owners). E-Class L: rattles and new-car odour.

## Cross-market signals for successor requirements

Candidate requirement areas, ordered by how consistently the evidence points the same way. These are inputs for the requirement pipeline, not finished requirements.

| # | Signal | Markets | Evidence strength | Forward-looking (3–5 years) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **Faster charging, better access to charging networks** | US, EU, CN | Strong: verdicts in all three markets, owner pain on both sides, spec gap | Rivals at 800–900 V and 10–15 min (CN). BMW's next-gen drivetrain (800 V, 400 kW, ~21 min) is announced and closes most of the gap |
| 2 | **Hands-free / navigate-on-autopilot driver assistance, standard rather than optional** | CN, US | Strong in CN, medium in US | L3 approved in China (Dec 2025), Huawei targets L3 at scale by 2027 |
| 3 | **Keep physical controls (rotary controller, climate keys) while the rest go touch-only** | EU, US | Medium: press praises iDrive, rivals criticised for touch-only | Audi (MY2027) and the new Lexus ES are bringing physical controls back |
| 4 | **Ride comfort and cabin quietness (air suspension) to match Mercedes** | EU, US | Medium: comparison tests and dB measurements | — |
| 5 | **Richer standard equipment per trim in China** (ventilation, sunroof, audio, connectivity included) | CN | Strong: 7 : 0 verdicts, recurring G68 owner complaints | NEV rivals add features by OTA updates |
| 6 | **Natural-language / LLM voice assistant** | all | Medium: trend, little owner voice yet | Volvo (Gemini), Mercedes (ChatGPT), BMW Alexa+ (DE/US, OS 9) and DeepSeek (CN) |
| 7 | **Software and electrical reliability** (screens, connectivity, brake-system software) | US | Medium: NHTSA on both sides (E-Class screen blackouts, 5 Series brake module) | — |
| 8 | **Protect what BMW wins on**: handling, build quality, boot space, efficiency | all | Strong: BMW leads head-to-head verdicts on these themes | — |

## Data quality and caveats

- **Thin owner voice outside China and US review sites.** EU owner forums and review sites are mostly blocked (Parkers, Honest John, motor-talk, Reddit, Edmunds, What Car, many forums behind paid bot gateways). Volvo ES90, Tesla Model S (EU), Audi A6 C9 and the 8th-gen Lexus ES have press records only.
- **Press dominates EU.** About 140 EU records come from ADAC alone. Count reviews (`review_ref`), not records.
- **Comparisons are not always against the G60.** Some refer to the G61 Touring, i4, i7 or the previous-generation G30; the statement names the model.
- **NHTSA**: almost all complaints are defects by design. Buckets are noisy (2023 EQE mixes sedan and SUV; text filter applied). Tesla's volumes reflect its fleet size, so compare shares.
- **China**: all owner reviews come from Sohu trim pages (Autohome renders reviews via JavaScript). Sohu snippets lean positive, and most reviews predate the latest updates (SU7 2026, ADS 4).
- **Conflicts to keep in mind**: Tesla Model S end of production (sources say May 2026 or late 2026), trunk volumes that differ between sources, and the ET7's CarPlay (catalogue says standard, tests say not available).
- **Quotes** come from WebFetch summaries and are not guaranteed verbatim; quotes ≥ 15 words were removed.
- BMW verbatim text is never stored, only IDs and labels.
